theme: The 144,000 and the great multitude; the seventh seal
readingInstruction: Read Revelation 7:1-8:13. Chapter 7 is an interlude between the sixth and seventh seals, answering the question “who can stand?” Chapter 8 opens the seventh seal and introduces the first trumpets. Notice the contrast between what John hears and what he sees.
settingTheScene: At the close of chapter 6, the world cries out, “who can stand?” Chapter 7 answers: the servants of God who are sealed. Like the pause in a symphony before the finale, this chapter shows the security of God’s people before the next round of judgments. It is also one of the most debated chapters in the book, because of the identity of the 144,000. Readers should note the pattern John uses elsewhere: he hears one thing and sees another (the Lion and the Lamb in chapter 5), so that the two parts interpret each other.
observation: “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads” (7:3).
“And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel” (7:4).
“A great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (7:9).
“Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (7:10).
“They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (7:14).
“For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water” (7:17).
“When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (8:1).
“The smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel” (8:4).
interpretation:
Four angels stand at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds. Another angel with the seal of the living God cries out, “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads.” The seal marks ownership and protection, the opposite of the mark of the beast later. Then John hears the number: 144,000, twelve thousand from each of the twelve tribes of Israel (with Dan omitted and Manasseh included in the list).

Who are they? Christians have given different answers. Some, especially dispensational interpreters, believe they are ethnic Israelites, perhaps converted Jews in a future tribulation. Others believe they are the church, the new Israel, the whole people of God described in the language of the old covenant, which the New Testament elsewhere applies to the church (Galatians 6:16; James 1:1; 1 Peter 1:1; Revelation 21:12-14). The number is twelve times twelve times a thousand, a symbol of completeness. The tribes are listed as an army ready for battle (Numbers 1-2), the sealed ones.

The next scene supports the second reading. “After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands.” As in chapter 5, John hears a number (the 144,000) and then sees a multitude beyond number. This echoes God’s promise to Abraham of descendants like the stars (Genesis 15:5; 22:17). It is the same people seen from two angles: Israel as an ordered army and the nations as a countless crowd. The multitude cries, “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” and the angels, elders, and creatures respond with a sevenfold doxology.

An elder asks, “Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?” And answers: “These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” This is a paradox: robes washed in blood become white. The great tribulation is understood by some as a future period at the end of the age, and by others as the whole age of the church’s suffering. Either way, those who endure are cleansed only by the blood of Christ. Their destiny is beautiful: “Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence. They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore… For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.” The Lamb is a shepherd, another paradox.

Chapter 8 opens the seventh seal. The result is silence: “there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” After the praise, a hush before the final events. Then seven angels are given seven trumpets. Another angel stands at the golden altar with a censer and “much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints.” The smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rises before God. Then the angel fills the censer with fire from the altar and throws it on the earth: thunder, lightning, earthquake. The prayers of the saints (like the martyrs’ cry in 6:10) are answered with judgment. The first four trumpets echo the plagues of Egypt: hail and fire mixed with blood burning a third of the earth; a burning mountain thrown into the sea; a star called Wormwood poisoning a third of the waters; a third of the sun, moon, and stars struck. These judgments are partial (a third), warnings meant to lead to repentance. An eagle flying overhead cries, “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth,” for three more trumpets remain.
connection: Ezekiel 9:4-6 and 2 Corinthians 1:22 speak of God’s seal. Ephesians 1:13 and 4:30 say believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit. Genesis 12:3, 15:5, and Romans 4:16-18 speak of Abraham’s multitude. Galatians 3:7-9, 29 and 6:16 call believers the Israel of God and Abraham’s offspring. Leviticus 23:40-43 and John 12:13 mention palm branches. Daniel 12:1 and Matthew 24:21 speak of great tribulation. Isaiah 25:8 and 49:10 are echoed in 7:16-17. Psalm 23:1-2 and John 10:11 show the shepherd. Habakkuk 2:20 calls for silence before the LORD. Exodus 7-10 recounts the plagues. Psalm 141:2 speaks of prayer as incense.
application:
Place yourself in the great multitude. Read 7:9-17 slowly, and thank Christ for washing your robes in his blood.

When you face a trial, recall verse 17: the Lamb is your shepherd, and he will wipe away every tear.

Pray with the confidence that your prayers rise before God like incense and are not lost.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for sealing and keeping his servants.
Thank him for a people from every nation.
Ask him to keep you faithful through tribulation.
